Consult Summary:
- 50-year-old woman with 5–6 days of persistent dry cough and rhinorrhea, with chills, fatigue, and myalgias; clinician impression of acute viral illness; supportive care advised.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Dry, continuous cough for 5–6 days, worse at night and disrupting sleep; associated runny nose.
- Associated symptoms: Chills/shivering at night (no recorded temperature), diffuse myalgias (arms/legs), lethargy/fatigue. Transient diarrhea at symptom onset (resolved). Throat irritation from coughing (no odynophagia). No chest pain. No day-to-day breathlessness. No nausea/vomiting. Ears without pain or discharge. Urination normal. Appetite okay. Partner asymptomatic.
- Pertinent negatives: No sputum production. No measured fever. No ongoing diarrhea. No ear pain/discharge. No chest pain. No exertional breathlessness reported.
- Past medical history: Type 2 diabetes; hypertension.
- Medications: Metformin (dose/route/frequency not documented). Lisinopril (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Allergies: No known drug allergies.
- Family history: Father with type 2 diabetes.
- Social history: Lives with partner. Works in IT (developer). Former smoker (quit ~6 months ago). Alcohol: wine, ~2–3 glasses up to 3 evenings/week; counseled to reduce.

Examination:
- Vitals: Not documented.
- Physical exam: Not documented.

Impression:
- Acute viral upper respiratory illness with dry cough and systemic symptoms (chills, myalgias, fatigue). No red flags by history; low concern for bacterial pneumonia at this time.

Plan:
- Supportive care: Rest; drink plenty of fluids; take acetaminophen (paracetamol) as needed for symptom relief (dose/frequency not specified).
- Work/activity: Take 1–2 days off for rest; consider returning early next week if improved.
- Follow-up:
  - Reassess if not improving in 2–3 days.
  - Return sooner if breathing worsens.
  - If fever persists and cough does not improve, clinician may consider antibiotics for possible chest infection.
- Lifestyle counseling: Reduce alcohol intake (suggested taper to ~2 glasses/week initially, with goal of further reduction), especially in context of hypertension and diabetes.
- Continue routine care for diabetes and hypertension with regular checks.

Quality checks:
● Missing expected elements: Vitals; physical exam; medication doses/routes/frequencies; vaccination/COVID status; sick contact history; baseline respiratory history (asthma/COPD); objective fever measurement.  
● Internal conflicts: Medication name—patient reported lisinopril; clinician repeated “Zinopril” (conflict noted).  
● Transcript quality: Some pauses/inaudible segments; no objective examination documented.
